content:
Laredo is the busiest land port in the United States, and the numbers keep climbing. Port Laredo recorded $353.94 billion in international trade in 2025 — a $14.94 billion increase over the prior year, according to data reported by WorldCity. But the boom has a cost, and Webb County residents feel it every rush hour on Loop 20.

Mayor Dr. Victor D. Treviño told the Texas MPO Association's annual meeting in Laredo last September that the port handles about $339 billion in trade annually and roughly 20,000 trucks a day, describing Laredo as the Western Hemisphere's top port of entry by value, according to Citizen Portal's AI-generated summary of the meeting. The figures were real — they described 2024 trade — but they are already out of date, and the superlative deserves a closer look.

Here is what the documented record shows. The Texas Comptroller's office puts 2024 trade through Port Laredo at $339.7 billion, supporting an estimated 1.1 million Texas jobs and contributing $135.2 billion to the state's GDP. Updated 2025 figures released this March show $353.94 billion — but they also carry a new WorldCity ranking that placed New York and Los Angeles ahead of Laredo among all U.S. ports, air, sea and land combined. As KGNS reported in February, Laredo dropped to No. 3 overall while remaining the No. 1 land port in the country. More than 97% of the port's trade is tied to Mexico.

The investments pouring in

City economic development director Miriam Castillo told the MPO audience that the metro population stands at roughly 300,000 — about 800,000 combined with Nuevo Laredo — and outlined a wave of industrial investment. The biggest: Stotan Industrial's Port Laredo Trade Center, a more than $100 million industrial park with 932,000 square feet across three buildings that broke ground in 2025 and was slated for completion in April 2026. The other marquee project: Mission Produce's $50 million mega distribution center — a 262,000-square-foot avocado and cold-storage hub that opened in 2021, reached about 110 jobs at full capacity, and helped pull roughly $120 million in produce and cold-storage investment and more than 450 jobs into the Laredo market. The LEDC's July 2025 newsletter also noted DSV inaugurating a major logistics facility in Laredo.

According to Castillo, the port's top commodity by value is motor vehicle parts, and electronic storage battery shipments have climbed markedly since 2016 — the nearshoring footprint is real, and it is growing.

The strain on the ground

The freight does not move through the abstract. Trade publication The Loadstar reported this month that daily truck crossings at Laredo range between 17,000 and 21,000 — consistent with the mayor's roughly-20,000 figure — and that the crossing handles about 40% of all U.S.-Mexico commercial traffic. But capacity is cracking: Uber Freight reports the pool of B1 drivers who haul freight from Mexico into the U.S. has shrunk by 25,000 since April 2025 amid enforcement of English-proficiency and cabotage rules, with backlogs of 30 to 50 loads hitting the Laredo crossing.

On the local roads, TxDOT's own project documents describe the Loop 20/Spur 400 intersection as highly congested at peak hours — motorists waiting through repeated signal cycles, with congestion delaying emergency vehicles. A Loop 20 expansion project was reported at about 40% completion late last year, and a $49.5 million overpass on the Cuatro Vientos corridor at Lomas Del Sur began construction in June 2025. The congestion is so severe it is reshaping public facilities: Lake Casa Blanca International State Park plans to move its main entrance off Loop 20 onto Ranchito Road — with 2,300 feet of queuing lanes — because holiday crowds back cars up onto the loop, with construction slated to begin in November 2027.

The watchdog question

The numbers in the mayor's pitch are documented — but they were 2024 numbers presented in September 2025, and "top port of entry in the Western Hemisphere" has quietly aged into "No. 1 land port." Watch what the framing does: it sells growth, not the cost of growth. Congressman Henry Cuellar told KGNS the tariffs contributed to Laredo slipping behind New York and Los Angeles, while Bridge Director Elsa Hinojosa pointed to high-value cargo like gold and medicine moving through the coastal ports. Either way, the narrative is doing political work while the balance sheet stays selective.

The harder question is distribution: who captures the boom, and who absorbs the cost. Developers and logistics firms are landing nine-figure projects. Meanwhile the people side of the region has stalled — Laredo's population growth fell to just 0.2% between 2024 and 2025, one of the sharpest slowdowns of any U.S. metro, according to Census estimates reported by KSAT. Freight is surging; the community is barely growing. And in Webb County's colonias, where basic water and sewer service is still the fight, there is no public accounting of how much port-driven revenue reaches the households that live closest to the truck routes.

"Act locally but think globally," the mayor told the planners. Webb Watch asks: when does the local part catch up?

excerpt: Laredo's port posted $353.94B in 2025 trade but slipped to No. 3 among U.S. ports. Up to 21,000 trucks a day strain Loop 20. Who's winning the boom — and who's paying?
title: Port Boom, Local Strain: Laredo Moves $354 Billion a Year — While Its Roads Choke
